young.html: On a stormy Scottish heath, three strange witches meet a brave general named Macbeth and tell him he will be king. Macbeth can't stop thinking about it. His wife, Lady Macbeth, wants it too, and pushes him on.

young.text:
Fair is foul, and foul is fair:
Hover through the fog and filthy air.
young.author: William Shakespeare
young.ed: First printed in the First Folio
young.note: Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

young.html: Macbeth does a terrible thing to become king. But one wrong leads to another, and the Macbeths can't sleep or rest. Lady Macbeth walks in her sleep, trying to wash away a spot that isn't there. In the end, the good lords of Scotland gather an army, and the rightful prince becomes king.

young.cap: Tap out the witches' beat, then Macbeth's. They speak in different rhythms.

young.html: For parents: Macbeth is a play about murder and guilt, with witches, ghosts and battles. It is short and gripping for older children, but some scenes are frightening. Young readers can start with Act I (the witches and the prophecy) and a retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

Chant like a witch. The witches speak in short lines with a strong DUM-da beat. Write four lines in that beat about something ordinary ("Dishes, dishes, in the sink, / Pots and pans and things that stink") and chant them together.

full.html: Macbeth (c. 1606) is Shakespeare's shortest tragedy. It is drawn from Holinshed's account of an 11th-century Scottish king, much changed. Shakespeare wrote it soon after King James VI of Scotland became James I of England; James had written a book about witchcraft and claimed descent from Banquo, whom the play treats with honor.

full.text:
I have no spur
To prick the sides of my intent, but only
Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself
And falls on th' other—
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.ed: First printed in the First Folio
full.note: He pictures ambition as a rider who leaps too hard into the saddle and falls off the far side. Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: Macbeth knows the murder is wrong: Duncan is his king, his kinsman and his guest, and a good ruler. Lady Macbeth questions his courage and his love, and he goes ahead. Before the deed he sees a dagger in the air.

full.text:
Is this a dagger which I see before me,
The handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee:—
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.ed: First printed in the First Folio
full.note: Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: Each crime leads to the next. Macbeth has Banquo killed and sees his ghost at a feast; he has Macduff's family killed. Lady Macbeth, once the stronger, walks in her sleep trying to wash invisible blood from her hands. By the end Macbeth feels almost nothing, and he speaks of life as a tale "signifying nothing."

full.cap: The prophecies of Act IV, and how they come true.

full.html: The witches never tell Macbeth to murder anyone. They only say what will be. The play leaves open how much is fate and how much is his choice, and that question drives it.
Blaming the witches or Lady Macbeth for everything. Macbeth is told the future, and urged by his wife, but every choice is his, and he knows it.

deep.html: Macbeth is full of images of blood, sleep, darkness and clothes that do not fit (borrowed robes, a giant's robe on a small man). The witches speak in a chanting trochaic beat, unlike anyone else; "fair is foul" turns up again in Macbeth's first line. Tracing these patterns is a good way to read the play closely.

items: If you were told you would get something you wanted, would you wait for it or try to make it happen?
Can a guilty conscience be escaped?
What makes a ruler a tyrant? How does the play show the difference between Duncan, Macbeth and Malcolm?

deep.html: Machiavelli's chapter on those who rise "by wickedness" (The Prince, Chapter VIII) is a good companion: such men, he says, may win power but not glory.

questions: The witches tell Macbeth what will happen, but not what to do. Who is responsible for what Macbeth does?
Why do you think one wrong act led Macbeth to another?
Lady Macbeth was braver than her husband at first, but guilt overcame her. What does guilt feel like, and what is it good for?
The witches say "Fair is foul, and foul is fair." When can something look good but be bad?
care: Macbeth is about murder, guilt and tyranny, with witches, a ghost and battles. This lesson summarizes the killings without detail and quotes nothing violent.
